kz_kyomi_kai.gf_detail: Not gluten-free. The restaurant's signature is buckwheat soba, and Japanese soba is almost always cut with wheat flour (nihachi style); the kaiseki courses also use wheat-based tempura, soy sauce, and dashi seasonings. There is no documented gluten-free menu or accommodation. This is not celiac-safe.
kz_kyomi_kai.vegan_detail: Not vegan. The fixed soba-kaiseki courses are built on seasonal seafood (sashimi, uni, conger eel), duck, dashi, and other animal ingredients. No vegan course or documented plant-based accommodation. As completely-reservation-based course-only dining, options are fixed by the kitchen.
kz_kyomi_kai.hours_raw: 12:00-14:00 (L.O. 13:00), 17:30-20:00 (L.O. 19:30). Closed Sundays and the first Monday of the month. Completely reservation-based (advance booking required).
kz_kyomi_kai.notes: [Mom & Pop] He opened Kyomi Kai in August 2015 in Kanazawa, his wife's hometown. The couple runs the small townhouse together.

chef_bio.origin: The chef is from Sendai in northeastern Japan; he trained at a culinary school in Tokyo and honed his craft in Yamagata and Tokyo.
chef_bio.background: He opened Kyomi Kai in August 2015 in Kanazawa, his wife's hometown. The couple runs the small townhouse together.
chef_bio.philosophy: Quiet, understated elegance: delicate course cooking that threads soba through each stage rather than serving it as a standalone bowl, letting seasonal local ingredients lead.
chef_bio.specialty: Soba kaiseki: refined seasonal Japanese courses with house-made buckwheat woven throughout, including coarse-ground sobagaki (buckwheat dumpling/cake), hand-cut soba noodles to finish, soba sushi, and dishes pairing soba with seafood such as conger eel, crab, and karasumi (bottarga).

anecdotes.text: The restaurant occupies a roughly century-old townhouse from the early Taisho era, fronted by Kanazawa's characteristic kimusuko wooden lattice, tucked in a back lane behind the Higashi Chaya geisha district.
A reviewer who balked at the per-person price before visiting came away astonished at the value compared with big-city dining, praising the airy, sake-lees-seasoned coarse-ground sobagaki.
Kyomi Kai earned a Michelin star (Toyama-Ishikawa 2016 and Hokuriku 2021) and is counted among western Japan's standout soba-and-kappō counters.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: food-japon.com and takemachelin.com confirm chef Tajiri Atsushi (from Sendai, trained Tokyo/Yamagata), the Aug 2015 opening in his wife's hometown, a husband-and-wife 10-seat early-Taisho machiya behind Higashi Chaya, the sake-lees coarse sobagaki, and Michelin one-star status (2016 Ishikawa, 2021 Hokuriku).

gf_cross_contamination.text: The kitchen centers on buckwheat soba (typically cut with wheat) plus tempura and soy/dashi seasonings, so wheat is pervasive across the fixed courses.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Courses are built on seafood, duck, and dashi; no plant-based course is documented and the menu is fixed by the kitchen.

cultural_comfort.note: A serene, formal course-only counter and table restaurant run by a married couple where reservations are essential and ordering is fixed; basic Japanese (or a Japanese-speaking helper to book) will make a foreign student's visit far smoother.

kz_gecko_do_curry_to_osake_.gf_detail: A spice curry shop where the curry base (clam broth with coconut milk, achaar, etc.) and accompaniments are not gluten-free and no gluten-free accommodation is documented. Spice curries here typically contain wheat-based thickeners and seasonings, and there is no published allergen handling. Not suitable for celiacs; if strictly gluten-free, ask in advance, but assume it is not safe.
kz_gecko_do_curry_to_osake_.vegan_detail: The rotating menu centers on seafood (shrimp, clams, scallops, salmon), chicken, egg, dairy (blue cheese), and clam/fish-based broths. No vegan or vegetarian option is documented. Not a vegan destination.
kz_gecko_do_curry_to_osake_.hours_raw: Sources differ after the 2025 reopening. Tabelog: Tue–Sat 11:00–14:00 & 18:00–21:00, Sun 11:00–14:00 (until sold out), closed Mon. A curry-guide source lists post-reopening lunch-only hours 11:00–15:00 (L.O. 14:30), closed Mon & Tue. Hours are subject to change; confirm via the shop's Instagram.

chef_bio.background: Gecko-do began as a curry shop in March 2020, born from a bar called GECKOS that the owner previously ran in Kanazawa's Shintenchi area. The owner runs the place solo out of a small converted house with a Showa-era exterior and an exotic, foreign-feeling interior tucked into a residential maze near Korinbo/Katamachi. In May 2025 the shop temporarily closed, but devoted regulars rallied to revive it, and it reopened in July 2025 keeping the original style and flavors.
chef_bio.philosophy: The owner cooks 'without attachment to the concept or conventional form of curry' — the guiding question is simply what tastes delicious, with each plate prepared individually rather than batch-cooked.
chef_bio.specialty: Spice curry that ignores convention, with a rotating lineup (often two varieties at a time). The standout is the Seafood Coconut Curry — shrimp, clams, scallops and butter-seared salmon over long-grain rice in a clam-broth-and-coconut-milk base, served with onion achaar and a boiled egg. Other rotating curries have included squid-ink seafood, chicken blue cheese, and chickpea-and-chicken. Guests are welcomed with hibiscus tea and offered several vinegars and condiments to vary the flavor mid-meal.

anecdotes.text: After the shop closed in May 2025, fans of Gecko-do came together to revive it, and it reopened on July 11, 2025 — just two months later — preserving the original taste and style.
The owner works alone and prepares each curry plate one at a time rather than in pre-made batches, so meals take extra time to come out.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: hokuriku-curry.com and food-japon.com confirm the shop grew out of the GECKOS bar in Shintenchi, opened as a curry shop March 2020, is run solo with each plate cooked to order, closed May 2025 and reopened 11 July 2025 via fan support, and serves a seafood coconut curry with hibiscus-tea welcome and table vinegars.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, owner-run hideaway in a converted house with little English signage and contact mainly by Instagram, so basic Japanese and an easygoing attitude help a lot.

kz_omicho_shunsai.gf_detail: This is a fish-market standing-drink counter run by a seafood wholesaler. Core items are sashimi, torched nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch), seafood bowls and a senbero (cheap drink) set, all of which lean on Japanese soy sauce — which is brewed with wheat — and there is no documented gluten-free menu, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling. Not celiac-safe; a celiac traveler would at minimum need to bring their own GF tamari and confirm in person.
kz_omicho_shunsai.vegan_detail: A seafood specialist whose entire menu is built around raw and grilled fish, oysters, sea urchin and scallops. There are no documented vegan or vegetable-only dishes; this is not a vegan-friendly destination.
kz_omicho_shunsai.hours_raw: Mon, Tue, Thu, Fri 10:00-15:00 / Sat, Sun & holidays 09:00-15:30. Closed Wed.

chef_bio.background: Tucked into a corner of Kanazawa's famous Omicho Market, this is the direct-run counter of Daimatsu Suisan, a long-standing local fish merchant. Because the same company sources the fish, the counter can put genuinely fresh seafood in front of you at market prices rather than restaurant markups. Until the summer of 2023 it operated as a robatayaki-style grill called Omicho Shunsai-yaki; that July the grill format was retired and the shop was renamed simply Omicho Shunsai, reframed as a casual standing spot so that, in the company's words, more visitors could taste what Daimatsu Suisan at Omicho has to offer.
chef_bio.philosophy: Let a working fish wholesaler's freshness speak for itself at an everyday, approachable price.
chef_bio.specialty: Torched nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch) aburi-sashi, raw oysters, sashimi platters, seafood rice bowls, and a signature senbero set pairing a draft beer with assorted sashimi and a small side for around 1,000 yen.

anecdotes.text: The popular senbero set comes with a draft beer, three kinds of sashimi and a small side dish for around 1,000 yen, making it an ideal quick market drink, with the torched nodoguro's fat melting just enough to pair beautifully with sake.
Open from around 9am (9:00-15:00), it's a casual stand-and-eat counter for fresh sashimi, grilled seafood and raw oysters, run directly by fish wholesaler Daimatsu Suisan.

With the July 2023 change of format the shop dropped its robatayaki grill and renamed itself Omicho Shunsai, centering the menu on the popular senbero set alongside raw oysters and torched nodoguro sashimi.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official Omicho Market page (9:00-15:00, closed Wed, a casual fishmonger-run counter) and Daimatsu Suisan's own news post confirm the July 2023 rebrand from the Shunsai-yaki grill to a standing spot centered on the senbero set, torched nodoguro and oysters. The retty review confirms the ~1,000-yen senbero set.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The menu centers on sashimi, torched nodoguro and seafood bowls, which are eaten with Japanese soy sauce (brewed with wheat); no wheat-free soy alternative is documented.
soy_sauce_wheat.why: Sashimi/炙りのどぐろ is supported; the soy-sauce sentence is not on the page in either direction. Either soften it to a stated assumption or cite a source that shows the condiment. Separately: the せんべろセット is built on 生ビール — barley beer is the loudest gluten item here and gf_detail does not name it.

vegan_cross_contact.text: An entirely seafood-based market counter (oysters, sea urchin, scallops, sashimi, nodoguro) with no documented plant-based options; cross-contact with fish is unavoidable here.

cultural_comfort.note: A bustling, no-frills market stand where two older women serve the counter and little to no English is expected, so a smile, pointing at the senbero set, and a few Japanese phrases will carry you a long way.

kz_dai_7_gyoza_no_mise.gf_detail: This is a gyoza (dumpling) specialty shop. The signature White Gyoza is defined by its thick, chewy wheat-flour skin, so the core menu is fundamentally wheat-based and not safe for celiacs. Dipping uses regular (wheat-based) soy sauce/vinegar. No gluten-free menu, dedicated fryer, or allergen accommodation is documented.
kz_dai_7_gyoza_no_mise.vegan_detail: The gyoza filling is meat-based (pork). This is a meat-dumpling specialist with no documented vegan or vegetable-only options; not suitable for vegans or vegetarians.
kz_dai_7_gyoza_no_mise.hours_raw: 1F 11:00-21:00 / 2F 11:00-21:00 / takeout 11:00-21:00 (shortened due to staff shortage). Official site lists 11:00-02:00, but Tabelog notes current shortened hours to 21:00.

chef_bio.origin: Kanazawa (もりの里, near Kanazawa University, beside the river)
chef_bio.background: A beloved Kanazawa gyoza institution affectionately known to locals simply as Dai-nana ("the 7th"). It belongs to the White Gyoza (ホワイト餃子) technical-chain lineage whose head shop is in Noda, Chiba, but it has become a soul-food landmark of Kanazawa in its own right, drawing long lines even on weekdays.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop frames itself as a specialist that can offer this distinctive product at low prices precisely because it focuses on gyoza alone, urging diners to eat them piping hot, fresh off the griddle.
chef_bio.specialty: Its signature is the White Gyoza: round, plump dumplings with a thick, chewy wheat skin that turns crisp and golden when deep-fried in oil. Around 90% of customers order them. The shop also serves steamed and boiled (water) dumplings and gyoza set meals at specialist-shop prices.

anecdotes.text: Locals call it simply 'Dai-nana' (the 7th), and roughly 90% of customers order the White Gyoza; the round, thick-skinned dumplings deep-fried to a crisp are its defining dish, often with waits of an hour even on weekdays.
The riverside upper-floor rooms offer seasonal views — cherry blossoms in spring, ayu fishing in summer, autumn foliage, and snow in winter.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: haraheri.net confirms the 'Dai-nana' nickname, ~90% White Gyoza order rate, thick-skinned deep-fried dumplings, and hour-long weekday waits; the official White Gyoza branch page confirms the Noda-Chiba technical-chain lineage and the riverside 2F rooms with spring cherry / summer ayu-fishing / autumn foliage / winter snow views.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Gyoza are fried/cooked in shared oil and equipment; the entire core menu is wheat-flour dumplings, so heavy gluten cross-contact is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard gyoza dipping sauce (soy sauce / vinegar / chili oil) is used; no gluten-free soy sauce is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dumplings are pork-based and cooked on shared meat equipment; no vegan options documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, no-reservation local gyoza counter where you can point at the famous round dumplings and order with a few words of Japanese, though expect a wait at peak times and little English.

kz_yakiniku_horumon_shibafu.gf_detail: This is a yakiniku/horumon (grilled beef offal) restaurant whose signature dishes revolve around house white and black sauces — the black sauce is a sweet-savory miso preparation — and a finishing bowl of wheat noodles. Soy- and miso-based marinades plus wheat noodles make this menu unsuitable for celiacs, and no gluten-free accommodation is documented. The site mentions allergy information is available, so a GF or wheat-sensitive diner should ask directly, but it is not a celiac-safe destination.
kz_yakiniku_horumon_shibafu.vegan_detail: The entire concept is grilled beef and beef offal (horumon, tongue, throat, heart). There are no documented vegan or vegetarian set offerings; the menu is built around meat. Not a vegan-friendly destination.
kz_yakiniku_horumon_shibafu.notes: [Mom & Pop] A compact horumon-yakiniku counter about three minutes' walk from the east exit of Kanazawa Station, just past the Tsuzumi-mon gate. The shop is built around a single idea: pursuing what it calls the ultimate way to eat meat.

chef_bio.background: A compact horumon-yakiniku counter about three minutes' walk from the east exit of Kanazawa Station, just past the Tsuzumi-mon gate. The shop is built around a single idea: pursuing what it calls the ultimate way to eat meat.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen frames good horumon as the mastery of five elements: the freshness of the meat, the sauce, the griddle, the grilling technique, and the finishing noodles.
chef_bio.specialty: The house Shibafu course is served in three movements — a 'white sauce' stage featuring premium cuts such as upper tongue and throat, a 'black sauce' stage of beef heart and offal dressed in a sweet-savory miso preparation, and a finishing bowl of special thick noodles designed to soak up the accumulated meat juices. Staff grill each piece individually in front of the diner using a tilted-griddle technique to lock in the juices.

anecdotes.text: The signature service is a tilted-griddle grilling method: rather than letting diners cook freely, staff grill each cut individually and tilt the plate so the flavorful juices are preserved and served at the optimal moment.
Sourcing prioritizes freshness, so the available cuts on the menu can change with what arrives.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: The official site (horumon-shibafu.com) confirms the location 3 minutes from Kanazawa Station's east/Kenroku-en exit, the five elements of good horumon, the three-part Shibafu course (white-sauce premium cuts, black-sauce miso offal, finishing thick noodles), and the staff-run tilted-griddle grilling technique.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Signature dishes center on house white and black sauces, the black being a sweet-savory miso preparation, and the meal ends with wheat finishing noodles — indicating soy/miso/wheat are integral and not avoidable.

cultural_comfort.note: The shop provides an English menu and supports reservations from international visitors, so a foreign student can dine here comfortably with minimal Japanese.

kz_nigokorei.gf_detail: No gluten-free information is documented. A celiac traveler should not assume any safe options; ask directly.
kz_nigokorei.vegan_detail: No vegan information is documented. Some menu items (matcha, certain anko-based sweets) may be plant-based, but souffle/cream items contain dairy and eggs, and no claims about vegan preparation exist. Ask staff about specific items.

chef_bio.background: Nigokorei is a quiet, antique-styled tea house tucked into Kanazawa's Nagamachi samurai-residence district, set inside an old wooden machiya said to be well over a century old (a reviewer recalls being told the building is around 140 years old). The space is filled with the atmosphere of old Japan, with seating arranged so guests can look out over a traditional interior garden (中庭).
chef_bio.philosophy: The proprietor places special emphasis on fine ceramics, particularly local Kutani ware, presenting tea and sweets in carefully selected vessels so the tableware is part of the experience.
chef_bio.specialty: Tea-house sweets served on carefully chosen pottery, including chestnut zenzai (栗入りぜんざい) made with nama-fu, a souffle set (スフレセット) with rich whipped cream, and ceremonial matcha.

anecdotes.text: The cafe is known for striking, eye-catching hina dolls displayed inside, adding to its distinctive retro atmosphere.
Visitors describe the chestnut zenzai's chewy nama-fu against rich, sweet anko, and a moist, gently sweet souffle that pairs well with coffee.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Tabelog's matome and shop reviews describe a Nagamachi machiya with a central garden, a proprietor devoted to Kutani ware, chestnut zenzai with nama-fu, a whipped-cream souffle set, matcha, and a display of hina dolls; the building age is only given loosely (one review recalls ~140 years, another guesses 200+).

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny, traditional owner-run kissaten in a 140-year-old house; little to no English is likely, so basic Japanese phrases and a calm, quiet manner will help.

kz_saboh_yanagian.gf_detail: No gluten-free program is documented. Some items (e.g. anmitsu with agar and azuki) may be naturally wheat-light, but cross-contact is unaddressed — a celiac visitor would need to ask in detail and should not assume safety.
kz_saboh_yanagian.vegan_detail: Not a vegan venue and no vegan menu is advertised. Some signature items are plant-based by nature (the gold-leaf cream anmitsu uses domestic agar, red bean paste and matcha warabimochi), but parfaits and afternoon-tea sets typically include dairy/cream and the kitchen is not vegan-oriented. A vegan would need to ask which items omit dairy/eggs.

roles: Operated by Hakuichi (箔一) gold-leaf brand
chef_bio.background: Saboh Yanagian is a second-floor wa-café inside 金澤しつらえ, a gallery-shop run by the renowned Kanazawa gold-leaf brand Hakuichi, set within a tea-house (chaya) building over 200 years old in the Higashi Chaya District. The space was restored on the floor plan of the former 'Kyū-Moroeya' era, when geisha performed their arts there, and blends period architectural design with contemporary touches — including a glass connecting corridor finished in gold leaf.
chef_bio.philosophy: The café aims to offer 'a quiet moment separated from everyday life,' inviting guests to feel as if they are dissolving into a Japanese painting while gazing at the historic streetscape.
chef_bio.specialty: Cream anmitsu crowned with a full sheet of gold leaf (applied tableside over soft-serve, agar jelly, fruit, matcha jelly and red bean paste), seasonal fruit parfaits, matcha served with Kanazawa wagashi in artisanal vessels, and seasonal afternoon-tea sets.

anecdotes.text: The café is named after the 'Mikaeri Yanagi' (backward-glance willow), the iconic tree standing right in front of the building and a symbol of the Higashi Chaya geisha district; table seats look out onto the swaying willow.

The building is a restored 200-year-old chaya once known as Kyū-Moroeya where geisha performed, and its second-floor connecting corridor was rebuilt in glass and finished with gold leaf, reflecting Hakuichi's gold-leaf craft heritage.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Hakuichi's official page and rurubu confirm a Hakuichi-run 2F wa-café in a 200-year-old Higashi Chaya chaya restored on the former Kyu-Moroeya (geisha-performance) floor plan, with a gold-leafed glass corridor, the Mikaeri-Yanagi namesake willow out front, and a signature gold-leaf cream anmitsu applied tableside.

cultural_comfort.note: A polished, tourist-friendly café in a famous gold-leaf brand's gallery; an English Tabelog page and card/QR payment exist, so a foreign student can visit comfortably with little Japanese.

kz_turban_curry_sohonten.gf_detail: Kanazawa curry is built on a dark, thick roux thickened with wheat flour and topped with breaded pork cutlet, so the food is wheat-heavy and not celiac-safe. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented.
kz_turban_curry_sohonten.vegan_detail: This is a meat-centric curry shop; signature dishes feature pork cutlet, sausage, hamburg steak, and a roux made with meat stock. No vegan or vegetarian options are documented.

chef_bio.background: Turban Curry was founded in 1971 (Showa 46), its first shop opening that August in Kanazawa's Katamachi, and has served its signature Kanazawa curry for over half a century, celebrating its 50th anniversary in August 2021. In August 2005 the flagship relocated to its current Hirosaka spot, near the 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art, where it continues as the sohonten.
chef_bio.philosophy: A streamlined, efficient counter operation focused on consistently turning out its rich, dark, medium-spiced curry rather than frills.
chef_bio.specialty: Classic Kanazawa-style curry: a thick, dark, glossy roux made with many spices, served over firm rice on a stainless-steel plate and typically ordered from a meal ticket. Signature plates include the L Set (pork cutlet, sausage, and hamburg steak together), pork cutlet (roskatsu) curry, and a house-made cream croquette curry, with takeout also available.

anecdotes.text: The founder of the now-famous Go Go Curry chain is said to have trained at Turban Curry's flagship before starting his own brand, placing this shop at the roots of the Kanazawa curry scene.
The shop marked its 50th anniversary in August 2021, half a century after its 1971 founding, and moved to the current Hirosaka storefront in 2005.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Wikipedia (カレーハウス・ターバン) confirms the 1971/Showa 46 founding with the first shop in Katamachi, the August 2005 relocation to Hirosaka while remaining the honten, and the Go Go Curry founder having trained at Turban; tacsp.net confirms the 50th anniversary (Aug 2021), the Hirosaka/21st-Century-Museum location, the meal-ticket counter service and firm rice.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Curry roux is wheat-flour based and the signature toppings are breaded/fried cutlets and croquettes, so wheat is pervasive throughout the kitchen.

cultural_comfort.note: A no-frills local counter curry shop with a quick, efficient ordering flow and cash-only payment, so come with yen and be ready to order promptly; a little guidance helps but the menu of cutlet/sausage/hamburg curries is easy to point at.

kz_noukabanzai_tonariya.gf_detail: Not gluten-free safe. The menu centers on nodoguro kamameshi finished as dashi-chazuke (broth poured over rice), and Japanese dashi/seasonings here typically involve soy sauce, which contains wheat. No gluten-free menu, dedicated preparation, or celiac accommodation is documented. Celiac travelers should avoid.

chef_bio.origin: Opened in 2021 inside Kanazawa's historic Omicho Market, on the Musashi side.
chef_bio.background: Tonariya is the nodoguro-kamameshi specialty shop of the local Noukabanzai brand, a Kanazawa group of several dining spots and a crafts shop built around Ishikawa (Kaga-Noto) regional ingredients. It puts the spotlight on nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch, akamutsu) — a fatty, refined white fish so prized it is nicknamed 'the toro of white fish.'
chef_bio.philosophy: A pared-back preparation that leaves nowhere to hide anything but the quality of the fish and the rice, letting the nodoguro speak for itself.
chef_bio.specialty: Nodoguro kamameshi: each clay pot is cooked to order from raw rice, taking about 20 minutes, forming a crisp okoge, and is served with a nodoguro broth gently drawn from the bones. The dish is designed to be eaten in three stages — first plain to taste the fish and crispy rice, then dressed up with ikura and condiments, and finally as dashi-chazuke with broth poured over the rice.

anecdotes.text: Nodoguro is described as a premium white fish whose fat is so refined it is likened to 'the toro of white fish,' and the kamameshi is meant to be enjoyed three ways: as-is with the crispy rice, with condiments and ikura, and as tea-soaked rice.
The nodoguro broth served alongside the rice is carefully made from the fish bones.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Noukabanzai's own page and the Omicho Market/kanazawabiyori guides confirm a nodoguro-kamameshi specialist in Omicho Market, cooked to order (~20 min) from raw rice with a crisp okoge and a bone-drawn broth, eaten three ways, and nodoguro praised as a refined white fish compared to fatty tuna. The exact opening date and marketing tagline were not source-confirmed, so they are phrased loosely.

cultural_comfort.note: A friendly single-dish counter spot inside the bustling Omicho Market where a basic greeting and pointing at the famous nodoguro kamameshi will get you through comfortably, though the staff and menu are primarily Japanese.

While some items use rice flour (米粉, e.g. banana bread), everything is baked in the same small shop with no dedicated gluten-free facility or stated allergen protocol, so cross-contamination with wheat is likely. Coeliac travelers should avoid the baked goods. Plain espresso/coffee drinks themselves contain no gluten.
kz_petra_bake_coffee.vegan_detail: Vegan-friendly options exist but the shop is not fully vegan. The bakery lists "animal-product-free" (動物性不使用) baked goods alongside conventional items so customers can choose what suits them, and soy milk is available for lattes (e.g. iced soy latte). However many baked goods contain dairy/eggs and the carrot cake contains walnuts, so ask which specific items are animal-free on the day. No claim of a fully separate vegan prep area.

It is the second venture from the team behind the well-loved MORON CAFE in the Nagamachi samurai district, bringing the same organic, homemade ethos into a compact grab-and-go space styled like an overseas cafe.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop deliberately bakes with as much organic flour as possible and offers a mix of rice-flour, spelt-wheat and animal-product-free items so that customers can pick what fits their own lifestyle and diet.
chef_bio.specialty: Homemade baked goods built around organic ingredients - a spelt-wheat carrot cake with walnuts, banana bread made with rice flour, plus cookies, muffins and scones - paired with espresso drinks. Signatures include the self-made spiced cafe mocha and an iced soy latte using aromatic espresso and smooth soy milk.

anecdotes.text: The espresso is a light-roast original blend sourced from the GOOD4LIFE 36CAFE coffee stand, chosen for a clean, gently sweet flavor.
It is the second location of Nagamachi's popular MORON CAFE, opened at the Omicho Market entrance to serve shoppers a quick, stylish break.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: weekend-kanazawa.com and the Omicho Market page confirm a May 21 2023 opening at the Omicho Market entrance (Aokusa-cho) as MORON CAFE's second location, an organic-leaning bakery with rice-flour, spelt and plant-based options, a spelt carrot cake with walnuts, rice-flour banana bread, and espresso from GOOD4LIFE 36CAFE with a signature spiced cafe mocha. (No gluten-free safety is claimed.)

gf_cross_contamination.text: Wheat, including spelt wheat (used in the carrot cake), is baked on-site alongside rice-flour items in a single small shop, so cross-contamination is likely; no dedicated gluten-free area is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Animal-product-free baked goods are offered on the same counter as dairy/egg items; no separate vegan prep is documented, and the carrot cake contains walnuts.

positives.text: The bakery explicitly offers animal-product-free (vegan) items and soy milk for lattes, so plant-based diners have real choices.
Some items are made with rice flour (米粉), such as the banana bread, giving non-strict diners lighter-wheat options.

cultural_comfort.note: A casual, stylish takeout coffee stand at the market entrance where pointing at the counter pastries and a few words of Japanese will get you through easily; staff likely have limited English but the order is simple.

kz_tsubajin.gf_detail: This is a traditional Kaga kaiseki ryotei built around wheat-based soy sauce, bonito/kombu dashi, and dishes like jibu-ni (which uses flour-dusted meat/fish) and tai no karamushi. There is no documented gluten-free menu, dedicated fryer, or celiac accommodation. Not safe for celiacs. A formal multi-course kaiseki cannot reasonably be made gluten-free here without prior arrangement, and no such accommodation is documented.
kz_tsubajin.vegan_detail: A 1752-founded ryotei specializing in Kaga cuisine built on fresh seafood (crab porridge, tai no karamushi, sashimi) and dashi-based dishes. Nothing vegan or vegetarian is documented on the official site or other sources. As a fully reservation-based kaiseki house with chefs who prepare bespoke courses, a vegan/vegetarian course might be possible only by arranging well in advance when booking, but it is not offered as standard and is not confirmed.

chef_bio.origin: Kanazawa (Teramachi, near Nomachi and the Saigawa river), Ishikawa Prefecture, Japan
chef_bio.background: Tsubajin is Kanazawa's oldest ryotei, founded in 1752 (Horeki 2). Its roots go back further: the Tsuba family served the Maeda clan of Kaga as hereditary tsuba (sword-guard) craftsmen from the late 16th century (the founder entered Kanazawa in 1583 as an armourer to Maeda Toshiie), and the third-generation Jinbei opened a small teahouse called Tsubaya alongside that trade, which grew into the restaurant known today as Tsubajin. The house has carried its craft of Kaga cuisine for roughly 260 years on its present footing as a restaurant.
chef_bio.philosophy: The house describes its enduring aim across some 350 years as flavors that satisfy and a heart that thinks of the guest, served entirely in private rooms.
chef_bio.specialty: Kaga regional cuisine served as kaiseki: signature dishes include jibu-ni (the representative Kanazawa stew), tai no karamushi (sea bream stuffed and steamed), hasu/renmushi (steamed lotus dishes), and a celebrated crab rice porridge (kani-gayu) breakfast. Courses use fresh local seafood and Kaga vegetables.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant has hosted many leading historical and literary figures, including the statesman Ito Hirobumi and the writer Akutagawa Ryunosuke.
Its name and lineage come from the Tsuba family's former trade as sword-guard craftsmen for the Maeda lords of Kaga before the family turned to cooking.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Traditional Kaga kaiseki built on wheat-based soy sauce and bonito/kombu dashi; signature jibu-ni traditionally uses flour-dusted protein, so gluten is intrinsic to the cuisine. No gluten-free preparation is documented.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Kaga cuisine here relies on standard Japanese soy sauce and dashi-based seasonings, which contain wheat; no wheat-free soy alternative is mentioned.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Menus center on seafood (crab porridge, sea bream, sashimi) and dashi; no vegan or vegetarian course is documented, so animal-derived stock and seafood are pervasive.

positives.text: Fully reservation-based with bespoke multi-course service, so dietary requests can in principle be raised when booking well in advance, though no specific accommodation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a formal, expensive, reservation-only historic ryotei with private-room kaiseki service and Japanese etiquette expectations; a foreign student should come with a host or guide, dress appropriately, and arrange any dietary needs far in advance.

kz_kissa_olive.gf_detail: A traditional kissaten whose menu centers on toast and sandwich sets (wheat bread) plus おしるこ; nothing indicates gluten-free options or any allergen handling, so it is not suitable for celiacs.
kz_kissa_olive.vegan_detail: Old-style coffee shop serving buttered toast, sandwiches and milk-based drinks; no vegan menu or plant-milk options are documented.
kz_kissa_olive.notes: [Mom & Pop] A long-running, old-fashioned kissaten tucked into the residential Nagamachi area near Kanazawa's samurai-house district and within reach of Omicho Market. It opens early at 7:30 in the morning, giving the neighborhood a quiet, unhurried place to start the day.

chef_bio.background: A long-running, old-fashioned kissaten tucked into the residential Nagamachi area near Kanazawa's samurai-house district and within reach of Omicho Market. It opens early at 7:30 in the morning, giving the neighborhood a quiet, unhurried place to start the day.
chef_bio.philosophy: A calm, classic kissaten atmosphere that welcomes both families and solo visitors.
chef_bio.specialty: Coffee is the heart of the shop, with around ten kinds of beans the owner selects and also sells, and toast and sandwich sets are the signature plates. House-made おしるこ (sweet red-bean soup) and a homemade honey-lemon drink round out the menu.

anecdotes.text: Regarded among Kanazawa's beloved retro kissaten, the shop is particular about its coffee and its sandwiches are singled out as especially good.
Known for toast sets generously topped with vegetables and fruit, plus homemade おしるこ and a complimentary honey-lemon service.

cultural_comfort.note: A quiet neighborhood kissaten run in the old-fashioned way with little to no English, cash only — easiest to enjoy if you bring a Japanese-speaking friend or are comfortable ordering by pointing.

kz_taishu_kappo_ozeki.gf_detail: This is a traditional oden and kappo izakaya built around dashi-simmered broth, eel with sauce glaze, and Kaga local dishes. The oden broth, the kabayaki-style eel sauce, and the simmered dishes all rely on wheat-containing soy sauce, and there is no dedicated gluten-free preparation. It is not a safe choice for celiacs. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented.
kz_taishu_kappo_ozeki.vegan_detail: The kitchen is centered on seafood, eel, crab, and fish-based dashi (the oden broth is made from herring/iwashi dashi). Nearly every dish involves animal stock or seafood, and there is no documented vegan or vegetarian menu. Not suitable for vegans or strict vegetarians.
kz_taishu_kappo_ozeki.hours_raw: 16:30-21:30 (Tabelog lists close 21:30; one local source lists last hours to 22:00). Closed Tuesdays (open on the eve of holidays).
kz_taishu_kappo_ozeki.notes: [Mom & Pop] Founded in December 1957 (Showa 32) in Kanazawa's Kikuramachi quarter near Katamachi and Korinbo, Ozeki is a long-loved neighborhood kappo-izakaya that still carries an authentic Showa-era atmosphere with its long oden counter and warm, homey feel.

chef_bio.background: Founded in December 1957 (Showa 32) in Kanazawa's Kikuramachi quarter near Katamachi and Korinbo, Ozeki is a long-loved neighborhood kappo-izakaya now run by the second-generation proprietor, 平吉晃 (Hirayoshi Akira). It still carries an authentic Showa-era atmosphere with its long oden counter and warm, homey feel.
chef_bio.philosophy: A welcoming, unpretentious neighborhood place where regulars gather at the counter; the proprietress is noted for creating a warm, homey atmosphere.
chef_bio.specialty: Kanazawa-style oden simmered in a refined, deep dashi broth (including seasonal items like crab face in November-December), and live-ordered freshwater eel prepared to the customer's choice of white-grilled, sauce-glazed, or combined. Kaga local dishes such as jibuni also feature.

anecdotes.text: The proprietor 平吉晃 prepares eel that is ordered live by the fish, combining Kanto-style back-cutting with Kansai-style grill-only cooking (no steaming) for a fragrant, crispy exterior and sweet fat.
On Mondays nearly all oden items are offered at a special low price (around 100 yen each), drawing crowds of regulars.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Oden, simmered dishes, and sauce-glazed eel are built on wheat-based soy sauce and fish dashi; there is no separate gluten-free preparation.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Eel is offered sauce-glazed (kabayaki style) and dishes use standard soy-based seasonings, which contain wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The oden broth and most dishes are made with fish/seafood dashi, and the kitchen centers on eel, crab, and seafood; vegan separation is not possible.

cultural_comfort.note: A cozy, old-school Showa-era counter izakaya where a little Japanese and an easygoing attitude go a long way; menus and conversation are mostly in Japanese, so a translation app helps for a foreign student.

kz_oden_wakaba.gf_detail: A traditional oden house built on a continuously replenished dried-sardine dashi seasoned in Japanese style; soy sauce (wheat-based) and miso are central, and items like tsumire and dote-yaki are not gluten-free. No gluten-free accommodation is documented. Not celiac-safe.
kz_oden_wakaba.vegan_detail: The entire menu rests on a fish (niboshi/sardine) dashi, and signature dishes include sardine tsumire, pork-belly dote-yaki, octopus and bay snails. There are a few plant-based oden items (daikon, taro, konnyaku, grilled tofu) but they are all simmered in the fish broth, so the place is not suitable for vegans.
kz_oden_wakaba.hours_raw: 17:00–22:00 (some listings note up to 22:30). Closed Mondays (and Tuesdays per Tabelog); first-come, first-served.

chef_bio.background: Founded in 1935 (Showa 10), Wakaba is one of the great old-school Kanazawa oden houses, tucked away in the residential Ishibiki neighborhood east of Kenrokuen rather than in the tourist quarters. It is run today by third-generation owner Yoshikawa Masashi, working alongside his father, the second-generation proprietor.
chef_bio.philosophy: Rather than chasing the modern 'Kanazawa oden' boom, the family deliberately keeps everything the same — their stated ethos is that they have never changed and never will, and that constancy is exactly why regulars keep coming back across generations.
chef_bio.specialty: Hand-made iwashi (sardine) tsumire — blended with onion and ginger, said to almost dissolve in the mouth while keeping a characteristic texture, and drinking up the broth; dote-yaki, simmered pork belly crowned with sweet white miso and a heap of minced green onion; plus Kanazawa classics like daikon, taro, octopus and bay snails. Everything bathes in a clear, lightly seasoned dashi built on a niboshi (dried sardine) base that has been continuously topped up since the shop opened.

anecdotes.text: The second-generation owner is the one who created the now-signature sardine tsumire, a recipe carried on by his son.
Prep starts around 9:10 in the morning so the pot is perfectly ready by opening, and the same broth has been replenished rather than replaced for decades.
The novelist Itsuki Hiroyuki (五木寛之), long associated with Kanazawa, was a regular and later wrote about the shop.

Diners sit at a single U-shaped counter around the bubbling pot, choosing items by sight; the atmosphere is unpretentious and mixes elderly regulars with younger groups, and solo guests are made to feel at ease.

gf_cross_contamination.text: All oden, including otherwise plant-based items like daikon and tofu, is simmered together in a shared fish-and-soy dashi, so cross-contact with wheat and fish is unavoidable.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The broth and seasoning are traditional Japanese soy- and miso-based, which means wheat-containing soy sauce; no wheat-free alternative is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The base dashi is made from dried sardines (niboshi), and every item shares that fish broth, so no dish is free of animal products.

cultural_comfort.note: A welcoming, populist old-school counter where even solo diners are made comfortable, but it is a traditional Japanese-only local spot, so a little Japanese (or pointing at the pot) will go a long way.

kz_coya.gf_detail: This is a wheat-flour bakery; bread is the entire product line. No gluten-free items, dedicated equipment, or allergy accommodations are documented. Not suitable for celiac or gluten-avoidant diners.
kz_coya.vegan_detail: A few of the signature items lean plant-forward — hard breads such as the raisin/currant loaf and Dainagon (red bean) stick may be made without dairy or egg — but the bakery also sells dairy/egg-rich goods (lemon cake, scones, cookies) and publishes no vegan labeling. Vegans would need to ask about each item; nothing is confirmed.

chef_bio.background: COYA. is a small bakery in the Oyama-cho neighborhood beside Oyama Shrine, run single-handedly by baker Ayako Tajiri. Its plain white-washed facade blends into the retro streetscape around the shrine. A 2019 renovation added a Sunday-only café space on the second floor, where coffee from a Toyama roaster is served alongside café-exclusive breads.
chef_bio.philosophy: Tajiri puts quality over quantity, baking only as much as she can make well each day and closing once it sells out. In her words she wants to keep making 'unpretentious bread you won't tire of even eating it every day,' letting the natural sweetness of the ingredients come through.
chef_bio.specialty: Hard-crust breads are the heart of the shop: a raisin-and-currant loaf, a Dainagon sweet-red-bean stick, and a chocolate baguette (choco-france). The house pain de mie comes in three styles — plain, sesame, and walnut — and draws daily regulars. The most talked-about item is the lemon cake, a French-style pound cake folded with lemon juice.

anecdotes.text: The owner refined her craft at Hiramipan (ひらみぱん), a celebrated Kanazawa bakery, before opening her own small shop.
A 2019 renovation introduced a Sunday-only second-floor café pouring coffee from a Toyama roaster, popular with both locals and tourists.
Decorative red peppers hang at the storefront as a charm to ward off misfortune.

gf_cross_contamination.text: A wheat-flour bakery where bread is the entire product line, so airborne flour and shared surfaces make cross-contamination unavoidable; not celiac-safe.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Dairy- and egg-rich items (lemon cake, scones, cookies) are made in the same small kitchen as the breads, so shared equipment is likely; no vegan separation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A tiny neighborhood bakery run single-handedly with no English signage — point at what you want, pay cash, and go early before the popular loaves sell out.

kz_shintate_bake_store.gf_detail: This is a wheat bakery — its entire identity is bread made from home-milled organic wheat and whole wheat flour. There is no gluten-free offering and it is not safe for celiacs.
kz_shintate_bake_store.vegan_detail: No documented vegan labeling. Breads use natural yeast and organic wheat; some items (canelé, cherry pie, pastries) clearly contain dairy/eggs. Simple lean breads may be plant-based but this is not confirmed, so vegans should ask about specific loaves.
kz_shintate_bake_store.hours_raw: 9:00-16:00 (closes earlier when sold out). Closed Monday and Tuesday.

chef_bio.background: Shintate Bake Store opened on April 12, 2023, in the Shintatemachi shopping street as the sister shop of the much-loved Kanazawa bakery Sakanoue Bakery (坂の上ベーカリー), run by the Wakai couple. In September 2023 the original Sakanoue Bakery closed and its bread workshop moved here, making Shintate Bake Store the continuation of that bakery's craft.
chef_bio.philosophy: The theme is 'healthy and delicious' (健やかで美味しく) — bread and sweets made with ingredients gentle on children, adults, and the environment, using pesticide-free organic wheat that is milled in-house and natural yeast. The owners deliberately do not serve coffee in the shop, encouraging customers to wander the shopping street and pair their bread with a drink from a neighboring cafe.
chef_bio.specialty: More than 20 kinds of bread and pastries are laid out daily from around 9 a.m., centered on breads made from home-milled organic whole wheat. Signature items include the Fukumitsuya canelé made with rice shochu from the local Fukumitsuya sake brewery, and the playful 'SS Cherry Pie' (a Twin Peaks reference, where SS stands for Shintate Street).

anecdotes.text: The shop intentionally avoids selling coffee so that customers will explore the Shintatemachi shopping street and combine the bread with offerings from nearby coffee shops.
It is the successor to Sakanoue Bakery: when that shop closed in September 2023, its bread workshop was relocated into Shintate Bake Store.

gf_cross_contamination.text: This is a flour-based bakery using home-milled organic wheat and whole wheat as its core ingredient; airborne flour and shared surfaces make it unsafe for celiacs.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Many items contain dairy and eggs (e.g. canelé, cherry pie); no separate vegan production is documented.

positives.text: Ingredients emphasize pesticide-free organic wheat and natural yeast with a 'healthy and delicious' philosophy, so the bread is made from carefully chosen, transparent ingredients.

cultural_comfort.note: A relaxed neighborhood bakery where you simply point at the bread you want and pay (cash or QR codes like PayPay accepted), so almost no Japanese is needed.

kz_ajidokoro_daikumachi_yos.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. This is a traditional Kaga kappo built on soy sauce and dashi, and the signature jibu-ni is thickened and includes fresh wheat gluten (sudare-fu/fu). No gluten-free menu or dedicated handling is documented; not safe for celiacs.
kz_ajidokoro_daikumachi_yos.vegan_detail: Not vegan-friendly. The menu is centered on Sea of Japan seafood (sashimi, sweet shrimp, nodoguro, snow crab) and meat (duck in jibu-ni), with dashi-based seasoning throughout. No vegan options are documented.
kz_ajidokoro_daikumachi_yos.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30-14:00 (reservation required), Dinner 17:00-22:30. Closed Sundays (and the following Monday when Sunday-Monday fall on consecutive holidays).
kz_ajidokoro_daikumachi_yos.notes: [Mom & Pop] Founded in 1977 in Kanazawa's Daikumachi quarter, a small street historically lined with kappo restaurants near the Saigawa river. The kitchen is now led by the second-generation proprietor, Yoshimura Ryoichiro, who cooks at the counter alongside a head chef in the classic kappo

chef_bio.background: Founded in 1977 in Kanazawa's Daikumachi quarter, a small street historically lined with kappo restaurants near the Saigawa river. The kitchen is now led by the second-generation proprietor, Yoshimura Ryoichiro, who cooks at the counter alongside a head chef in the classic kappo style.
chef_bio.philosophy: A 'quality over quantity' ethos inherited from the previous generation: the chef goes to market daily to hand-pick fresh fish, Kaga vegetables and local ingredients, keeping more than 70 seasonal dishes available so guests can eat omakase-style at the counter.
chef_bio.specialty: Kaga cuisine and Sea of Japan seafood. Signatures include jibu-ni (duck and Kaga vegetables with fresh wheat gluten in a thick sauce), Kaga lotus-root dishes such as hasu-mushi (steamed lotus) and lotus-root soup, sashimi of squid, sea urchin, sweet shrimp and konbu-cured fish, and seasonal specialties like hamo with matsutake and snow crab in winter.

anecdotes.text: A reviewer budgeting around 10,000 yen reported a course that ran about 11,000 yen yet far exceeded expectations in portion size and ingredient quality, singling out an exceptional abundance of matsutake with hamo and a creamy Kaga lotus-root soup.
The signature first-floor seating is a vermilion lacquered counter, where the appeal is watching the chef work and chatting casually while seasonal Kaga dishes are served.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Traditional Kaga kappo cooking relies heavily on soy sauce and dashi, and the house signature jibu-ni includes fresh wheat gluten (fu) and a flour-thickened sauce, so gluten is pervasive in the kitchen.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Japanese soy sauce (wheat-containing) is used throughout Kaga cuisine and its signature dishes here; no wheat-free soy sauce is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen is centered on seafood and meat with dashi-based seasoning; no separate vegan preparation is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a traditional family-run kappo where you sit at the counter and chat with the chef; reservations and some basic Japanese (or a translation app) will make the experience much smoother for a foreign student.

kz_nodoguro_meshi_honpo_ita.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. The food centers on grilled fish over seasoned rice eaten with condiments and a finishing dashi broth, which typically rely on wheat-containing soy sauce and dashi seasonings. No gluten-free menu or celiac handling is documented; not suitable for strict celiacs.
kz_nodoguro_meshi_honpo_ita.vegan_detail: Not vegan. This is a fish specialty shop built around nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch), yellowtail and other Kaga seafood, with fish-bone dashi broth. There are no documented vegan dishes.
kz_nodoguro_meshi_honpo_ita.hours_raw: Lunch 12:00-14:30, Dinner 17:30-20:30 (L.O. 20:00). Note: some listings show lunch-focused hours of 11:30-16:30/17:00 (L.O. 16:30). Hours vary by source/season — confirm by phone.

chef_bio.origin: Kanazawa, Ishikawa — a homegrown offshoot of the city's Itaru izakaya group.
chef_bio.background: A specialty shop devoted almost entirely to one dish — nodoguro-meshi, a bowl of premium blackthroat seaperch. It belongs to the locally beloved Kanazawa group '酒と人情料理 いたる' (Sake and Heartfelt Cuisine Itaru) founded by Ishiguro Itaru, and the original nodoguro-meshi shop opened on the day the Hokuriku Shinkansen reached Kanazawa in 2015. In February 2021 it relocated from Kakinokibatake to the Korinbo area, into a building originally constructed in 1964 (the year of the Tokyo Olympics) and lovingly renovated.
chef_bio.philosophy: Owner Ishiguro Itaru wanted the relocated shop to feel like a welcoming hatago (traditional travelers' inn), evoking an inn his family once ran. He filled the interior with heirlooms, including Inami wood carvings and paintings left by his late father.
chef_bio.specialty: Nodoguro-meshi (3,300 yen): generously piled, aromatically grilled nodoguro over seasoned rice, eaten in three stages — first plain, then with condiments, and finally as ochazuke with a rich, cloudy broth simmered from nodoguro bones. Other dishes include a sesame yellowtail bowl (ゴマぶり丼), and handmade sweets such as umeboshi-filled 梅つつみ.

anecdotes.text: When the shop moved to Korinbo in 2021, the owner designed it as a nostalgic 'hatago'-style retreat and decorated it with family heirlooms — Inami wood carvings and his late father's paintings.
The signature nodoguro-meshi is meant to be savored in three escalating stages, finishing with a cloudy soup extracted from the nodoguro's own bones poured over the rice.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes are seasoned-rice fish bowls finished with condiments and a fish-bone dashi broth; these preparations conventionally use wheat-containing soy sauce and dashi seasonings, so the menu is not safe for strict gluten avoidance.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Entirely seafood-based (nodoguro, yellowtail, Kaga fish) with fish-bone broth; no vegan options are documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A popular, tourist-friendly seafood-bowl shop with tablet ordering and card/QR payments; a little Japanese helps but you can manage with basics and pointing at the famous nodoguro bowl.

kz_coffee_dokoro_nobaru.gf_detail: A classic Showa-era kissaten whose menu centers on pudding, parfaits, cakes, napolitan pasta, and sandwiches, all wheat- and dairy-based. No documented gluten-free offering and no allergy accommodation. Not suitable for celiac diners.
kz_coffee_dokoro_nobaru.vegan_detail: The signature items (custard pudding with fruit and whipped cream, pudding parfaits, cakes) rely heavily on eggs and dairy, and the cafe also serves napolitan and sandwiches. No vegan or plant-based options are documented.
kz_coffee_dokoro_nobaru.hours_raw: 9:00-19:00; closed Wednesdays. Hours and holidays may change, so check before visiting.

chef_bio.background: A long-loved retro coffee house near the Arimatsu intersection, Nobaru has been operating for more than 40 years. It is run by a husband-and-wife team, the master and the mama, and its brick exterior and Showa-era interior, with stained-glass partitions casting soft light, have remained almost unchanged since it opened.
chef_bio.philosophy: The seating is laid out so that sight lines between customers are calculated to keep others unobtrusive, creating a relaxed space where guests can linger comfortably.
chef_bio.specialty: The signature is the homemade firm-set custard pudding (around 500 yen): the master makes the pudding by hand and the mama decoratively cuts fruit and adds whipped cream on top. It is gently sweetened so it pairs well with coffee or tea. A pudding parfait is praised for its generous volume, and the cafe also serves classic kissaten fare like napolitan, sandwiches, cakes and breakfast sets, with most items under 1,000 yen.

anecdotes.text: Actress Yoshida Yo is said to have worked part-time at this cafe when she lived in Kanazawa in her younger years, which has added to its local fame.
The interior is nearly unchanged from when it opened, with stained-glass partitions that cast soft, reflective light, making it a popular photography spot.

cultural_comfort.note: A warm, family-run retro coffee house where the master and mama greet regulars; little to no English, so a few words of Japanese or pointing at the menu will make your visit smooth.

kz_tokubetsu_meisho_kenroku.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. The signature dishes are jibu-ni (a stew thickened with wheat flour and seasoned with wheat-based soy sauce), plus udon and soba, all containing wheat. Sweets like dango and ankoro-mochi use rice flour but are served with soy-based or sweet sauces. No gluten-free menu, labeling, or accommodation is documented. Not suitable for celiacs.
kz_tokubetsu_meisho_kenroku.vegan_detail: This is a Kaga-cuisine teahouse centered on jibu-ni (duck/meat stew) and seafood (sweet-shrimp rice bowl), so the savory menu is not vegan. However, as a 甘味処 (sweets house) it offers matcha tea, plum juice, soft-serve, and dango/ankoro-mochi sweets — some of which may be plant-based but are not verified vegan (sauces and dashi unconfirmed). No declared vegan menu. A vegan visitor could likely have matcha and certain sweets only; confirm ingredients with staff.
kz_tokubetsu_meisho_kenroku.hours_raw: 9:00–16:30 daily (lunch service to ~14:30). Seasonal: 9:00–17:00 (Mar 1–Oct 15), 9:00–16:00 (Oct 16–end of Feb). Dinner by reservation only, extended during illumination and cherry-blossom seasons. Tabelog lists 08:15–17:00.

chef_bio.background: Tsutsumitei was founded in 1888 (Meiji 21) and occupies a building more than a century old on the historic tea-shop street of Kenrokuen, one of Japan's three great landscape gardens. With its calm, russet-walled rooms and second-floor tatami chambers overlooking the garden, it has served generations of visitors near the Katsurazaka entrance and Kanazawa Castle's Ishikawa Gate.
chef_bio.philosophy: A traditional teahouse experience: enjoy regional Kaga cuisine and Japanese sweets in a historic garden setting, with veranda seating for a quick matcha and dango or upstairs rooms for a full meal.
chef_bio.specialty: Kanazawa's signature Kaga dish jibu-ni (a stew of duck/meat and vegetables), served on its own or as jibu-ni udon and soba; also a sweet-shrimp rice bowl. As a sweets house it is known for matcha, homemade-sauce dango, ankoro-mochi (sweet bean-paste rice cakes), seasonal parfaits, soft-serve, and house-made plum juice.

anecdotes.text: The shop safeguards carved wooden statues of the prosperity deities Daikoku and Ebisu as family heirlooms, made from timber salvaged from the historic Saikawa Bridge during its 1918 reconstruction.
On the first floor the shop sells local souvenirs, crafts, Kaga-yuzen textiles, and regional sake, while the second-floor tatami rooms serve meals with garden views.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Jibu-ni is traditionally thickened with wheat flour and seasoned with wheat-based soy sauce, and the menu prominently features udon and soba; assume wheat is present throughout the savory offerings.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen centers on duck/meat jibu-ni and seafood (sweet-shrimp bowl); dashi and broths likely contain animal products, so even vegetable or sweet items may share preparation surfaces.

positives.text: As a 甘味処, matcha tea, plum juice, and rice-based sweets (dango, ankoro-mochi) are available, giving non-meat diners some options alongside the savory Kaga dishes.

cultural_comfort.note: A welcoming tourist-oriented teahouse inside Kenrokuen where you can point at picture menus and order matcha or jibu-ni with just a few words of Japanese; a friendly greeting goes a long way.

kz_kenrokutei.gf_detail: Not gluten-free friendly. The signature dishes are built on wheat: jibu-ni dusts chicken/seafood in wheat flour before simmering in dashi, and the house "jibu soba" uses noodles that contain wheat (standard soba is a buckwheat-wheat blend). Soy-based dashi and seasonings are used throughout. No gluten-free menu or accommodations are documented. Celiac travelers should not consider this safe.
kz_kenrokutei.vegan_detail: Not a vegan destination. The cooking centers on chicken, seafood (sea urchin, nodoguro, sushi), Noto beef, and dashi stock. No vegan or vegetarian set menus are documented. A vegan diner could potentially ask about the cafe (sweets, matcha lattes, local teas), but wagashi and dairy lattes are not reliably plant-based and nothing is confirmed. Best to treat as ask-only with very limited prospects.
kz_kenrokutei.hours_raw: Breakfast 9:00–11:00 (reservation required, by 3pm previous day); Lunch 11:00–14:00; Cafe 9:00–16:30 (to 16:00 in winter); Evening "Genan" dining 18:00+ by reservation, light-up season only. Open year-round per one listing; official site notes irregular closures.
kz_kenrokutei.notes: Kenrokutei occupies one of the most enviable addresses in Kanazawa: inside Kenrokuen Garden, looking out over what is said to be Japan's oldest fountain. chef_bio.background: Kenrokutei occupies one of the most enviable addresses in Kanazawa: inside Kenrokuen Garden, looking out over what is said to be Japan's oldest fountain. The kitchen is led by a chef who trained at a well-regarded Kyoto establishment, and the place leans on that pedigree while staying rooted in Kaga's own food culture.
chef_bio.philosophy: The cooking emphasizes handmade, additive-free dishes built on seasonal local vegetables and seafood, served in a calm room with garden views.
chef_bio.specialty: The house specialty is an original "jibu soba" — the classic Kaga dish jibu-ni reimagined over noodles, with crisp roasted chicken and Kaga renkon (lotus root) worked into the soba. The broader menu runs through jibu-ni sets, seafood rice bowls (sea urchin, nodoguro), Noto beef sukiyaki, and hand-rolled sushi, alongside a garden cafe of wagashi, matcha lattes and local teas.

anecdotes.text: Beyond daytime dining, the same address transforms in the evening into a private dining room called Genan (幻庵), where guests can take a kaiseki course while looking out over the illuminated garden during light-up season.
The signature jibu soba kneads crisp roasted chicken and Kaga lotus root into the noodles, turning the regional braise jibu-ni into a noodle dish unique to this house.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Jibu-ni is prepared by dusting chicken and other ingredients in wheat flour before simmering, so wheat is integral to the signature cooking and shared prep surfaces.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Dishes rely on dashi and Japanese seasonings (soy-based), and the signature soba contains wheat alongside buckwheat; no wheat-free preparations are documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen centers on chicken, seafood, beef and dashi; vegetable and cafe items are prepared in the same kitchen with no documented vegan separation.

positives.text: An English menu is available, which can help travelers communicate basic needs even though no formal allergen program is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: An English menu is available and the garden setting draws many overseas visitors, so a foreign student can order comfortably here.

kz_jardin_paul_bocuse.gf_detail: No documented gluten-free program. This is classic French cuisine where flour-thickened sauces, bread, and wheat-based preparations are central, so it is not celiac-safe. Allergy consultations are accepted at the time of reservation, so a guest could ask, but cross-contamination cannot be assumed to be controlled.
kz_jardin_paul_bocuse.vegan_detail: A vegetarian menu is available, but it must be arranged in advance at reservation. There is no documented fully vegan menu, and as a French kitchen built around butter, cream, dairy, and seafood/meat stocks, vegan diners should confirm a fully plant-based course directly when booking rather than assume it.
kz_jardin_paul_bocuse.hours_raw: Lunch 11:30–15:00 (L.O. 13:30); Dinner 17:30–22:00 (L.O. 20:00). Closed Mondays (or the following day if Monday is a holiday).
kz_jardin_paul_bocuse.notes: Jardin Paul Bocuse occupies the second floor of Shiinoki Geihinkan, the former Taisho-era Ishikawa Prefectural Government building in central Kanazawa, restored as an elegant guesthouse near Kenrokuen. It opened in 2010 and is one of only two places (alongside Tokyo) carrying the

chef_bio.background: Jardin Paul Bocuse occupies the second floor of Shiinoki Geihinkan, the former Taisho-era Ishikawa Prefectural Government building in central Kanazawa (Hirosaka), restored as an elegant guesthouse near Kenrokuen. It opened in 2010 as Hokuriku's Paul Bocuse grande maison, inheriting specialties from the celebrated main restaurant in Lyon, France.
chef_bio.philosophy: A fusion of Lyonnaise gastronomic tradition with the bounty of Ishikawa, set in a historic building accented with Kanazawa cultural touches such as gold leaf and yukitsuri motifs.
chef_bio.specialty: Classic Lyonnaise French specialties handed down from the Paul Bocuse main restaurant, combined with seasonal French dishes built around Ishikawa and Hokuriku seafood and produce.

anecdotes.text: In Japan the specialties of the Paul Bocuse main restaurant can be enjoyed at only two places — here in Kanazawa and at Tokyo's Maison Paul Bocuse (opened 2007 in Daikanyama).

staff_allergy_handling.text: Allergy consultations are accepted at the time of reservation.

positives.text: A vegetarian menu is available with advance arrangement.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a polished fine-dining French restaurant inside a historic guesthouse that hosts international guests and offers online reservations in English, so a foreign student would be comfortable, though the price point makes it a special-occasion choice.

kz_ryotei_otomoro.gf_detail: Traditional Kaga kaiseki built on dashi and soy sauce (which contains wheat), with wheat-thickened jibu-ni and various wheat-containing components. No gluten-free menu, no dedicated handling, and nothing about celiac safety is documented. Not suitable for those who must strictly avoid gluten.
kz_ryotei_otomoro.vegan_detail: A seafood- and dashi-centric formal Kaga cuisine ryotei; signature dishes are sea-bream and the duck/seafood stew jibu-ni, and stocks are bonito/fish based. No vegan or vegetarian menu is documented. As a fully reservation-based ryotei it may be possible to request a customized course in advance by phone, but this is not advertised and would need to be arranged ahead.

chef_bio.background: Otomoro is a long-established Kanazawa ryotei founded in 1830 (Tenpo 1), whose family long served as cooks to the Maeda lords of the Kaga domain. Over generations it has preserved the refined, ceremonial cooking of the castle town. When Kanazawa Station opened in 1898 the house began producing railway bento, and it continues to run a bento shop and prepared-foods counter alongside its formal dining rooms.
chef_bio.philosophy: To carry forward Kanazawa's culinary heritage by pursuing the elegance, aroma and beauty of traditional Kaga cuisine, using carefully selected seasonal ingredients and meticulous handwork while offering heartfelt hospitality.
chef_bio.specialty: Traditional Kaga cuisine, above all jibu-ni (a duck/seafood stew thickened and simmered in a savory broth) and tai no karamushi (steamed sea bream), served in seasonal kaiseki courses.

anecdotes.text: The family served as cooks to the Maeda lords of the Kaga domain, and the house has carried that castle-town cuisine forward since its founding in 1830.
Its tea room Isseian occupies a roughly 250-year-old building that once served as a place of tea instruction for Kaga-domain samurai.
The restaurant began selling station bento when Kanazawa Station opened in 1898, beginning a long railway-food tradition.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: Official site (ootomorou.co.jp) states 創業天保元年 (founded Tenpo 1 = 1830), long service as Maeda-family chefs, station-bento sales from Kanazawa Station's 1898 opening, the ~250-year-old Isseian tea room once a Kaga-domain tea-instruction hall, and jibu-ni / tai-no-karamushi as house dishes.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Traditional Kaga kaiseki here relies on soy sauce and dashi-based seasoning; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and the signature jibu-ni is traditionally thickened with wheat flour.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Cooking is centered on fish/bonito dashi and seafood (sea bream, jibu-ni), so plant-only dishes are not part of the documented menu and shared stocks would be used throughout the kitchen.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a formal, completely reservation-based heritage ryotei with multi-course kaiseki at high prices, so a foreign student would be most comfortable visiting with a Japanese-speaking guide or host who can book and explain the courses.

kz_ajidokoro_takasaki.gf_detail: This is a traditional Japanese restaurant whose cooking relies heavily on soy sauce, dashi, and Kaga local dishes like jibuni (which is typically thickened/seasoned with soy and often dusted with wheat flour). No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented, and there is no dedicated fryer. Not safe for celiacs.
kz_ajidokoro_takasaki.vegan_detail: The menu is built around seafood (nodoguro, crab, oysters, gas shrimp), duck (jibuni), and fish-based dashi. No vegan or vegetarian offering is documented; this is a seafood-and-meat washoku destination, not suitable for vegans.
kz_ajidokoro_takasaki.hours_raw: Mon-Sat 17:00-22:00 (L.O. 21:30). Closed Sundays (except three-day holiday weekends), year-end/New Year.
kz_ajidokoro_takasaki.notes: A long-running Kanazawa washoku restaurant, established in 1971, set near the Nagamachi samurai district just off Korinbo. Over more than half a century it has built its reputation on Kaga regional cooking and the seafood of the Sea of Japan.

chef_bio.background: A long-running Kanazawa washoku restaurant, established in 1971, set near the Nagamachi samurai district just off Korinbo. Over more than half a century it has built its reputation on Kaga regional cooking and the seafood of the Sea of Japan.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen keeps preparation as simple as possible to let the natural flavor of carefully sourced ingredients come through (素材本来の味を生かす為、調理はできるだけシンプルにして), aiming to make refined Kanazawa cuisine approachable.
chef_bio.specialty: Nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch, grilled or as sashimi), Ishikawa snow/Kano crab, natural rock oysters, white gas shrimp sashimi, the house crab-cream croquette, and Kaga local dishes including jibuni (duck simmered in soy-seasoned broth). Seasonal lineup spans firefly squid and gas shrimp in spring, rock oysters and Kaga vegetables in summer, hairy crab and sweet shrimp in autumn, and Kano crab and winter yellowtail in winter.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant frames its food around the seasons of the Sea of Japan and the Kaga region, rotating its centerpiece dishes through firefly squid in spring, rock oysters in summer, hairy crab in autumn, and prized Kano crab in winter.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: food-japon.com/p/takasaki and the gnavi listing confirm a 1971-founded Nagamachi/Seseragi-dori washoku restaurant, its 'keep prep simple' philosophy, and a seasonal menu built on nodoguro, Kano crab, rock oysters, gas shrimp and the crab-cream croquette.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Cooking is centered on Kaga local dishes such as jibuni and a range of simmered and grilled preparations that conventionally use soy sauce and dashi; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The menu is dominated by seafood, crab, duck and fish dashi, so vegan dishes and the avoidance of animal-based stock are not accommodated.

cultural_comfort.note: A traditional, well-established kappo-style washoku restaurant where a few words of Japanese and a phone reservation will smooth your visit; staff are used to tourists but it is an evening dining destination rather than a casual drop-in.

kz_shokudo_tsuki.gf_detail: This is a Japanese seasonal cuisine izakaya built around sashimi, simmered and grilled seafood, and sake. Dishes rely heavily on dashi and Japanese soy sauce (which contains wheat), and there is no documented gluten-free menu or allergy program. Not suitable for celiacs.
kz_shokudo_tsuki.vegan_detail: The menu centers on fresh fish and seafood (sashimi, anago, uni hand rolls) with daily market catch as the core draw, and dashi-based seasoning throughout. No vegan or vegetarian offering is documented.
kz_shokudo_tsuki.notes: [Mom & Pop] Shintani grew up around cooking — his father was a professional chef and his siblings also went into the trade — and he entered the kitchen himself at age 15. chef_bio.background: Shintani grew up around cooking — his father was a professional chef and his siblings also went into the trade — and he entered the kitchen himself at age 15. He trained in hotels and traditional ryokan and worked his way up to head chef at the popular Katamachi izakaya 'Sho' before going independent and opening Shokudo Tsuki in April 2022. He is a certified sake sommelier (kikisake-shi).
chef_bio.philosophy: The name 食道 ('the path of food') reflects his wish to roam freely across genres rather than be boxed into formal washoku, balancing respect for tradition with playful creativity. He wants guests to drop in casually and spend a relaxed, unfussy evening.
chef_bio.specialty: Daily-changing seasonal Japanese cooking driven by what he hand-picks at the market each morning, with fresh fish at the heart of the menu. Signature plates include seasonal sashimi (季節の鮮魚のお造り), a chilled simmered-anago bowl, grilled yanagi-sawara finished with sudachi, and a raw Hokkaido (Nemuro) uni hand roll that regulars have followed him from his 'Sho' days as a favorite closing dish. He pairs these with local sake sourced from across Japan.

anecdotes.text: The raw uni hand roll using Hokkaido Nemuro uni has been a customer favorite since Shintani's time at the izakaya 'Sho', and longtime guests still order it as their finishing dish.
Shintani came from a cooking family — his father was a professional chef and his siblings also pursued culinary careers — and he started in the kitchen at 15.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The cooking is traditional Japanese seafood cuisine relying on dashi and soy-sauce-based seasoning, which in Japan normally contains wheat; no gluten-free accommodation is documented.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The menu is built around fresh fish and seafood with dashi-based seasoning; no vegan or plant-only dishes are documented.

cultural_comfort.note: This is a local counter izakaya where ordering and conversation happen in Japanese, so a little Japanese or a translation app will help a foreign student feel comfortable.

kz_ohguchi_suisan_yakiyaki_.gf_detail: This is a grilled-seafood and sushi counter where items like salt-grilled nodoguro, scallops and squid are likely fine on their own, but no gluten-free handling is documented, soy-based sauces and shared grills are in use, and staff are not set up for celiac-level allergy management. Not safe for strict celiacs.
kz_ohguchi_suisan_yakiyaki_.vegan_detail: A seafood-focused grilled counter run by a fishmonger; the menu is built entirely around fish, squid, scallops, shrimp and eel. There are no vegan options.
kz_ohguchi_suisan_yakiyaki_.hours_raw: 9:00–15:00 (per Omichō Market official page); some listings show 9:00–17:00. Closed Wednesdays.
kz_ohguchi_suisan_yakiyaki_.notes: [Mom & Pop] The Yakiyaki Corner is the grilled-seafood standing counter of Ohguchi Suisan, one of the largest and longest-running fishmongers in Kanazawa's 300-year-old Omichō Market, which holds the biggest sales floor in the market. chef_bio.background: The Yakiyaki Corner is the grilled-seafood standing counter of Ohguchi Suisan, one of the largest and longest-running fishmongers in Kanazawa's roughly 300-year-old Omichō Market, with one of the market's biggest sales floors. Alongside its fresh-fish cases, the shop runs an open grill where market-fresh seafood is skewered and cooked right in front of customers to eat on the spot.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop leans on ingredients pulled straight from the market's own fish counters, aiming for affordable, market-fresh seafood eaten casually on the spot.
chef_bio.specialty: Charcoal-grilled skewers from about 200 yen each — squid legs, scallops, salt-grilled nodoguro (blackthroat seaperch), eel liver, Noto-region fugu and shrimp — plus fresh sashimi and sushi packs (sushi offered on Sundays and holidays), often washed down with a 350-yen draft beer.

anecdotes.text: Skewers such as scallop, squid and eel liver are grilled to order right in front of you, making it a favorite stop for eating while strolling the market.
A 350-yen draft beer alongside 200-yen skewers makes it an easy, affordable pause in the middle of the market.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: ohmicho-ichiba.com shop page for Ohguchi Suisan lists skewers from 200 yen (squid legs, salt nodoguro, scallop, eel liver, Noto fugu, shrimp), 350-yen draft beer, 500-yen crab soup, and fresh sushi on Sundays/holidays, all grilled to order at the market counter.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Skewers are cooked on a shared open grill alongside marinated and sauced items, so cross-contact with wheat-containing sauces is likely.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Sashimi and sushi are served, which are typically eaten with standard (wheat-containing) soy sauce; no gluten-free soy sauce is documented.

positives.text: Salt-grilled items such as nodoguro shioyaki and plain salted scallops are grilled simply with salt rather than sauce.

cultural_comfort.note: A bustling open-air market counter where you point at the skewer you want and eat standing up; a few words of Japanese and pointing go a long way, and English is unlikely.

kz_goryori_igarashi.gf_detail: This is a traditional Kaga kaiseki/kappo kitchen built around dashi, soy sauce, and seasonal seafood — all of which involve wheat-based seasonings (regular soy sauce contains wheat). There is no gluten-free menu and no documented allergen handling. Not suitable for celiacs.
kz_goryori_igarashi.vegan_detail: A seafood- and Kaga-vegetable-focused seasonal kaiseki restaurant serving fixed omakase courses. Fish, dashi (typically bonito/kombu), and animal products are central to every course; there is no vegan menu and dishes cannot meaningfully be made vegan. Not a vegan destination.
kz_goryori_igarashi.notes: [Mom & Pop] The chef behind this small Seseragi-dori counter spent nine years training at the celebrated Asadaya ryotei in Kanazawa, then served nine more years as head chef at Lamp no Yado in Suzu, the famed seaside ryokan on the Noto Peninsula, before opening his own place in May 2014.

chef_bio.background: The chef behind this small Seseragi-dori counter spent nine years training at the celebrated Asadaya ryotei in Kanazawa, then served nine more years as head chef at Lamp no Yado in Suzu, the famed seaside ryokan on the Noto Peninsula, before opening his own place in May 2014.
chef_bio.philosophy: He cooks for contrast and season — temperature, flavor and texture, seasonality, and the cleverness of combinations — and deliberately keeps prices approachable so that this level of craft stays within reach.
chef_bio.specialty: Seasonal Kaga kaiseki built on local seafood and Kaga vegetables, served as fixed omakase courses — refined cooking that plays with temperature, texture, and seasonal pairings.

anecdotes.text: He runs the whole kitchen single-handedly, turning out a long, intricately composed sequence of dishes alone — a feat regulars marvel at.
Tucked into a single-story wooden house on Seseragi-dori, where a clear canal runs past year-round, the room is just a six-seat counter facing the open kitchen and a handful of small tables.
Despite elaborate plating and unexpected touches, the courses remain modestly priced — a point reviewers single out as unusually generous.

chef_bio.japanese_sources_summary: food-japon.com/p/igarashi: 9 years at Asadaya ryotei, then 9 years as head chef at Lamp no Yado in Suzu (Noto), opened May 29 2014 on Seseragi-dori in Korinbo; one chef runs the kitchen; ~6 counter seats plus four two-tops; prix-fixe at 6,000/8,000/10,000 yen, praised as generous for the craft.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Traditional kaiseki built on dashi and soy-based seasonings; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and there is no documented gluten-free handling.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Courses are seafood- and dashi-centric with animal products in nearly every dish; no plant-only option is documented.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, quiet owner-run counter where the chef serves set omakase courses — comfortable for a student with some Japanese who can phone ahead to reserve, but there's likely little English and no menu choices to point at.

kz_hickory.gf_detail: A Showa-era kissaten whose signature dishes are curry omurice, fried rice, cheese toast and parfaits — wheat-based bread, roux, and flour are central to the menu.
